title: Rhythm and Groove
intro: Groove is the repeating rhythmic feel that makes people move: the tempo, how the beat is divided, where the accents fall and how the instruments lock together. Choosing it early shapes everything else in a song.

blocks.text: Tempo sets the energy: ballads around 60–80 BPM, mid-tempo pop 90–110, dance music 120–130, punk 160 and up. Feel is how the beat divides: straight (even eighths or sixteenths), swung or shuffled (long–short pairs), or in triplets (6/8, 12/8). The same chords and melody can sound like a ballad, a shuffle or a march depending on the feel (see Syncopation, Tuplets and Polyrhythm (#/arts/music-theory/rhythm/syncopation-and-polyrhythm)).

items: Rock and pop: kick drum on 1 and 3, snare backbeat on 2 and 4, eighth notes on the hi-hat. Guitar and piano often play straight eighths or a syncopated push into beat 3.
Ballad: half-time feel (snare only on 3), long sustained chords, broken-chord piano or fingerpicked guitar.
Funk: sixteenth-note subdivision, tight syncopated guitar 'chicken scratch', bass and kick locked on the 'one'.
Shuffle and blues: swung eighths, the boogie bass pattern (root–fifth–sixth–fifth).
Bossa nova: a syncopated two-bar pattern in the guitar's chords over an alternating bass (root, fifth) on the thumb.
Waltz (3/4): one strong beat per bar of three quarter notes, usually bass on 1 and chords on 2 and 3.
6/8 and 12/8 ballads: a pulse every three eighths; slow blues, doo-wop and many slow rock ballads use 12/8.

widget.title: The same C–Am–F–G in three feels (piano)

blocks.text: Anticipating a chord change by an eighth note (playing the next chord on the 'and' of 4) is one of the most common moves in pop and rock: it gives forward motion without changing the chords. In melodies, syncopated phrases that start just after the beat sound conversational; phrases that land squarely on beats sound declarative, which suits a chorus.

In a band the bass usually follows the kick drum and the chordal instruments fill the spaces around the snare. In a duo of piano and guitar, one instrument should own the rhythmic pulse while the other plays longer notes or answers between phrases (see Piano and Guitar Together (#/arts/songwriting/piano-and-guitar-together)).

items: Play one four-chord loop at three tempos and in straight and swung feel; note which suits your melody.
Write a rhythm for the chords first (strumming or comping), then improvise a melody over it.

blocks.text: Sources: London, J. (2012). Hearing in Time, 2nd ed. Oxford University Press; Perricone, J. (2018). Great Songwriting Techniques. Oxford University Press; Pressing, J. (2002). Black Atlantic rhythm: its computational and transcultural foundations. Music Perception 19(3).
